Redwood SE to produce sizing and burst strategy doc (Ravi)
Customer to share traffic profile, p95 latency SLOs, and sensitive dataset types (Karen)

action_items: Ava Martinez: Send pricing + commitment tiers by 2026-03-06

summary: Discovery focused on Dedicated reserved GPU capacity: isolation requirements, burst/bursting strategy, scaling expectations, compliance (SOC2/KMS), and pilot next steps.
topics: Sizing (A100 vs H100) and cost tradeoffs
transcript:
00:00:00 - Meeting start / intro
Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Ava Martinez from Redwood, with Ravi our SE. How's it going?
00:00:06 - Karen: Good, thanks. Appreciate you fitting us in. We wanted to dig into Dedicated — we have strict isolation needs and predictable costs.
00:00:14 - Ravi (Redwood SE): Great. High level we'll cover reserved GPU pools, autoscale/burst options, network / VPC connectivity, and compliance. Quick question: what's your target model family and SLOs?
00:00:26 - Daniel (CTO): We're evaluating a 70B-class model for summarization and QA across customer documents. Need p95 latency under 400ms for short prompts, and throughput up to ~200 rps at peak, spikes to 500 rps for short windows.
00:00:40 - Maya (Infra): And we need data isolation — logs and inference artifacts must never leave our VPC, keys under our KMS, plus audit logs for regulatory review.
00:00:50 - Ava: Perfect — that's exactly the Dedicated conversation. We can provide reserved GPU pools in your VPC (or a private deployment). For keys we integrate with customer KMS/HSM — you can manage keys and control access.
00:01:02 - Ravi: On the runtime side, Redwood's serving runtime supports H100/A100 mappings; for a 70B you can run quantized or FP16 depending on quality/latency needs. We'd recommend H100 for tighter p95, A100 for cost savings if you can tolerate slightly higher latency.
00:01:22 - Karen: For isolation — do we need a private deployment on-prem, or can Dedicated with VPC peering satisfy auditors?
00:01:30 - Ava: Most enterprise customers use Dedicated with a customer-controlled VPC peering and a private control plane. That gives you network-level isolation and customer-managed KMS. Private on-prem is available if auditors demand air-gapped.
00:01:44 - Daniel: How does bursting work? Our traffic is spiky — end of quarter runs push 3x baseline for an hour. We can't afford tail latency spikes.
00:01:54 - Ravi: There are a few patterns. Reserved capacity sizing covers your baseline; we offer burst capacity as either pre-warmed spare GPUs in the same pool or cloud burst to Redwood Hosted/compatible variants. Pre-warmed gives the best latency but costs more in commitment. The hosted fallback is cheaper but can add variability and cold-starts for heavier models.
00:02:14 - Maya: Do you autoscale automatically? We need predictable upper bounds.
00:02:18 - Ravi: Yes, autoscaling is configurable by policy. You can set strict max instance counts, queue time SLOs, and a warm pool threshold. For predictable budgets, customers often set a guaranteed baseline (reserved) plus a capped burst budget.
00:02:31 - Ava: We'll include pricing options for reserved capacity with and without pre-warmed burst — that should give you both price predictability and a plan for spikes.
00:02:40 - Karen: Sounds good. Also, curious about caching and KV cache — you mentioned prefix caching could reduce cost.
00:02:48 - Ravi: Right. Redwood supports KV cache/prefix caching; it reduces token compute for repeated contexts. For QA workloads with a lot of repeated context, caching can reduce effective GPU load significantly and lower required reserved capacity. Note: transcription sometimes shows it as 'KV cash' in quick notes.
00:03:04 - Daniel: What about model rollouts and fallbacks? We need canary testing and instant rollback if quality degrades.
00:03:10 - Ravi: We support version pinning, canary routes, and automatic fallback to a smaller model variant if latency/throughput thresholds are breached. You can also route only a percentage of traffic to a new model for comparative evals.
00:03:22 - Maya: Network topology — will we do VPC peering or PrivateLink? Any constraints on IPs or egress?
00:03:28 - Ava: Both are supported. We'll share a network diagram and recommended firewall rules. For stricter setups customers use PrivateLink and restricted egress with strict routing.
00:03:38 - Karen: Compliance: does Redwood provide SOC 2 reports, pen test results, and logs for audits?
00:03:44 - Ava: Yes — SOC 2 Type II and we can share a redacted penetration test summary. Audit logs for inference requests and admin actions are available and can be exported to your SIEM.
00:03:56 - Daniel: Let's talk numbers — what does a commit look like for our scale (200 rps baseline, 500 rps spikes)?
00:04:03 - Ravi: We'll take your traffic distribution and run a sizing exercise. Quick estimate: if average tokens per request are ~150 and you want sub-400ms p95, a conservative starting point is a small pool of H100s sized to handle baseline with a 30% headroom and a burst pool to handle spikes. Exact GPU counts depend on batching, sequence lengths, and quantization. We'll provide a model-by-model mapping.
00:04:26 - Ava: We'll include both A100 and H100 pricing scenarios and an ops plan: baseline reserved, capped burst, and fallback to hosted.
00:04:34 - Maya: On encryption, we need customer-controlled KMS and disk encryption on any attached volumes.
00:04:40 - Ravi: Supported — we integrate with KMS for key wrapping and can enable disk encryption. For on-prem, you can bring your own HSM.
00:04:47 - Karen: Any gotchas for evals/benchmarks? We need reproducible latency tests.
00:04:52 - Ravi: For reproducibility, we run a perf harness with representative prompts and synthetic traffic matching your QPS profile. We'll run both steady-state and spike tests. We'll log end-to-end latencies and token-level breakdowns so you can verify p95 and p99.
00:05:06 - Daniel: How do you handle model updates and version drift? We have model governance requirements.
00:05:11 - Ravi: You can pin versions for production; rollouts are explicit. Redwood also provides drift monitoring and eval hooks so you can run regression tests against your prompt sets before promote.
00:05:21 - Karen: Security team will want SAML/SSO and RBAC.
00:05:24 - Ava: We support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls with audit trails.
00:05:30 - Maya: Is there any data residency support in Dedicated? We have EMEA customers.
00:05:34 - Ava: Yes, Dedicated deployments can be regional and we support data residency controls. We'll capture region requirements in the SOW.
00:05:42 - Daniel: Cost sensitivity — how does per-token cost compare to reserved pool cost?
00:05:47 - Ravi: Reserved capacity is effectively a committed GPU hourly rate for throughput; per-token on hosted is variable. For heavy sustained workloads, reserved capacity is almost always cheaper per effective token. We'll model both in the pricing spreadsheet.
00:06:00 - Karen: Any performance tuning we should plan for?
00:06:03 - Ravi: Yes — batching parameters, KV cache strategy, quantization profiles, and kernel selection (we'll handle kernel selection) — all can be tuned. We'll propose initial defaults then iterate after pilot runs.
00:06:18 - Ava: Quick clarification: you mentioned 200 rps baseline — is that sustained across the day or bursty?
00:06:24 - Karen: Sustained midday traffic of ~200 rps with spikes to 500 during certain events. Request size is typically 80-200 tokens.
00:06:33 - Ravi: Good. That helps sizing. Also ask: are there any heavy long-context requests?
00:06:38 - Daniel: Occasionally — 2-3% of requests are multi-page contexts (~2k tokens).
00:06:44 - Ravi: We'll factor those into pre-warmed capacity or separate long-context workers to avoid impacting short-request p95s.
00:06:52 - Karen: One other question — SLA and uptime?
00:06:55 - Ava: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets aligned to the commit level. We'll include SLA text in the docs we send.
00:07:04 - Maya: How are incidents handled?
00:07:07 - Ava: 24/7 on-call for enterprise SLAs, escalation paths, and designated CSM/Support channels.
00:07:12 - Daniel: Ok let's talk pilot — what would you need from us to run a 2-week pilot?
00:07:18 - Ravi: Representative traffic traces, sample prompts, SLO targets, and access to a staging VPC or allow Redwood to spin up a pilot VPC with peering. We'll run a baseline perf harness first.
00:07:30 - Karen: We'll extract logs and traffic histograms — should be able to share by Friday.
00:07:34 - Ava: Awesome. We'll follow up with pricing, SOC 2, and a proposed pilot plan.
00:07:40 - Daniel: Anything else?
00:07:43 - Maya: One small thing — can you quantify what pre-warmed vs cold-start latency looks like for H100 with our expected payloads?
00:07:50 - Ravi: Roughly, pre-warmed H100 median for short prompts is ~80-120ms with p95 under 300ms depending on batching. Cold starts for big models can add 1-4s if a model shard needs to be loaded; that's why pre-warmed is recommended for critical paths. We'll include numbers in the sizing doc.
00:08:08 - Ava: Perfect. Let's recap next steps. We'll send pricing and a sizing doc, SE will run a sizing estimate and propose burst approach, Karen will provide traffic profile and tokens.
00:08:18 - Karen: Sounds good. Thanks both.
00:08:21 - Ava: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the deck and pilot proposal.
00:08:25 - Meeting end (call lasted approximately 48 minutes)

Notes about transcript: occasional transcription glitches (names and acronyms), timestamps approximate every few minutes, speakers sometimes overlap.
